subject: Physics
description: Lenses (convex/concave): focal length, magnification, image properties, lens applications in cameras, telescopes, eyes, microscopes.

questions.stem: A convex lens forms a real, inverted, and magnified image of an object. Where must the object be placed?

options.option_text: At focal point F itself alone

questions.explanation: CONVEX LENS — image properties depend on object distance: (i) Object at INFINITY → image at F, real, inverted, highly diminished (a point). (ii) Object beyond 2F → image between F and 2F, real, inverted, DIMINISHED. (iii) Object AT 2F → image at 2F, real, inverted, SAME SIZE. (iv) Object between F and 2F → image beyond 2F, real, inverted, MAGNIFIED ← matches the question. (v) Object AT F → image at infinity, undefined. (vi) Object between F and lens → image on same side, virtual, erect, MAGNIFIED (magnifying glass). KEY FORMULA: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (sign convention: distances measured from optical centre; f positive for convex). REAL-WORLD: SLIDE PROJECTORS work in setting (iv) — film slide is between F and 2F so we get a magnified inverted image (the slide is loaded upside-down to invert back). EYE LENSES: human crystalline lens is convex, focal length ~22 mm, focuses real images on retina. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing the standard ray-diagram/image-table — appears in NCERT Class 10 ch. 10.

questions.stem: A concave lens always produces an image that is:
questions.explanation: CONCAVE (diverging) LENS — regardless of object position, image is ALWAYS: (1) on the SAME SIDE as object (virtual); (2) ERECT (upright); (3) SMALLER than object (diminished); (4) BETWEEN F and the optical centre. Why? Concave lens diverges parallel rays, so they appear to emerge from a virtual focal point on the SAME side as the incident light — image cannot form on opposite side. KEY FORMULA: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (f is NEGATIVE for concave); magnification m = v/u always less than 1. REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS: (a) Spectacles for MYOPIA (short-sightedness) — concave lens diverges light entering the eye, shifting the focal point back to the retina. (b) Peephole/door-viewer (combined with convex). (c) Galilean telescope's eyepiece. PYQ ANGLE: NCERT Class 10 PYQs test exactly this 'always diminished' nature. EXAM TRAP: students confuse with concave MIRROR (which can give real magnified images) — concave LENS is fundamentally different.

questions.stem: The power of a lens is +5 dioptres. What is its focal length and type?
questions.explanation: POWER P = 1/f (where f is in METRES). P = +5 D → f = 1/5 = 0.20 m = 20 cm. POSITIVE power = converging = CONVEX lens. NEGATIVE power = diverging = concave. UNIT: dioptre (D) = m⁻¹. EYE-PRESCRIPTION ANGLE: when an optician writes '−2.50 D' for your spectacles, that's a concave lens of focal length 1/2.5 = 0.40 m = 40 cm to correct myopia. '+1.50 D' = convex, 67 cm focal length, corrects hyperopia. CAMERA LENSES: a 50mm camera lens has f = 0.05 m → P = 20 D — a 'fast' lens. ZOOM lenses combine multiple convex/concave elements; effective P shifts as elements move. INSIGHT: lens-maker's equation 1/f = (n−1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) means thicker lenses = shorter f = higher power. A 'plus 5' lens means it bends light enough to converge parallel rays at 20 cm — useful for reading glasses and small magnifiers. EXAM TIP: convert dioptre↔metres carefully; mistakes always come from forgetting the metres convention.

questions.stem: A simple microscope uses which type of lens, and what kind of image does it produce?

options.option_text: Convex lens producing virtual magnified image

questions.explanation: A SIMPLE MICROSCOPE (magnifying glass) is a single CONVEX lens of short focal length. Object placed BETWEEN F and the optical centre → image is VIRTUAL, ERECT, MAGNIFIED — viewed comfortably at the near point (~25 cm). MAGNIFICATION formula: M = 1 + D/f, where D = least distance of distinct vision (25 cm). For f = 5 cm → M = 1 + 25/5 = 6×. COMPOUND MICROSCOPE: uses TWO convex lenses (objective + eyepiece) for higher magnification (~1500× max for light microscopes). HISTORY: Anton van Leeuwenhoek (Dutch, 1670s) built ~270× single-lens microscopes and discovered bacteria, sperm cells. INDIA NOBEL TRIVIA: C.V. Raman discovered Raman scattering using a similar setup (lenses + spectroscope). LIMIT: optical microscopes can't resolve below ~200 nm (diffraction limit, Abbe's law). For finer detail, electron microscopes (~0.1 nm resolution). EXAM ANGLE: NCERT Class 10 lens applications — staple PYQ.

questions.stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Where does the image form?

options.option_text: 60 cm on opposite side of lens

questions.explanation: LENS FORMULA: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. SIGN CONVENTION (Cartesian): u is NEGATIVE (object on left, light goes right), f POSITIVE for convex. Plug: 1/v − 1/(−30) = 1/20 → 1/v + 1/30 = 1/20 → 1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = (3−2)/60 = 1/60 → v = +60 cm. Positive v means image on the OPPOSITE side (right), real and inverted. MAGNIFICATION m = v/u = 60/(−30) = −2 → image is 2× and inverted. INSIGHT: object at 30 cm (= 1.5f) lies between F and 2F, so we expect a real, inverted, magnified image beyond 2F (= 40 cm) — answer 60 cm matches that prediction perfectly. PROJECTOR APPLICATION: this exact setup (object near 2F) is used in slide projectors for screen-size magnification. EXAM TIP: Cartesian sign convention is the SSC/IBPS standard — object distance ALWAYS negative when light travels left-to-right.

questions.stem: Which defect of vision is corrected by a CONVEX (converging) lens?
questions.explanation: VISION DEFECTS — quick map: (1) MYOPIA (short-sight) → eye too long OR lens too convex → image forms BEFORE retina → fix with CONCAVE lens (diverges incoming light). (2) HYPERMETROPIA / HYPEROPIA (far-sight) → eye too short OR lens too flat → image forms BEHIND retina → fix with CONVEX lens (converges to bring image forward to retina). (3) PRESBYOPIA = age-related hypermetropia from lens stiffening (~age 40+); fixed with reading glasses (convex) or bifocals. (4) ASTIGMATISM = cornea is non-spherical (cylindrical) → fixed with CYLINDRICAL lens. (5) CATARACT = lens becomes cloudy → fixed by SURGERY (replaced with synthetic IOL — intraocular lens). INDIA STAT: ~80% of preventable blindness in India is from cataract; ~6 million surgeries/year. PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC, RRB Group D include vision-defect Qs every 2-3 cycles. NCERT CLASS 10 — Ch. 11 covers all of this. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing whether you can map a defect to its physical cause AND its corrective lens.

questions.stem: Two thin lenses of powers +3 D and −1 D are placed in contact. What is the power of the combination?
questions.explanation: LENSES IN CONTACT: powers ADD algebraically. P_total = P₁ + P₂ + … For thin lenses in contact (separation d≈0), this simple addition holds. P = +3 + (−1) = +2 D. The combination acts as a CONVEX lens (positive power). FOCAL LENGTH: f = 1/P = 1/2 = 0.5 m = 50 cm. WHY? Each lens contributes its own bending; the second lens picks up where the first left off. Mathematically: 1/f_combined = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂. APPLICATION — ACHROMATIC DOUBLET: a convex crown-glass lens (+) glued to a concave flint-glass lens (−) — combined power positive but cancels chromatic aberration (different colours focusing at different points). Used in high-end telescopes, microscopes, camera lenses. INVENTOR: John Dollond (1758, England). PYQ ANGLE: lens-combination Qs appear in CGL Tier 1 every 2-3 sessions; both qualitative ('which type') and quantitative ('what power'). KEY: this is also why eye prescriptions can correct multiple defects at once — combined lens powers.
